introduction-the-nightmare-of-shared-sta.core: Threads that share mutable memory need locks, and locks bring deadlocks, races and contention that grow worse with every core. The actor model takes a different route: nothing is shared. State is private to an actor and changes only through messages, which the actor handles one at a time, so concurrency lives in the message queue instead of in locks.

first_principles.problem: A multi-threaded order book deadlocks under load because two threads take the same pair of locks in opposite order.
truths: A single owner needs no lock.
derivation: Give each piece of state **one owner**.
Process messages **one at a time** per owner.
Scale by adding **more owners**, not more threads per owner.

analogy.title: Desk clerks with in-trays
analogy.story: Nobody grabs papers off a clerk's desk. You drop a note in their tray and they handle notes one by one.
analogy.breaks: Clerks can shout across the room; actors only ever exchange messages.

example.title: Bank account
flow: Thread version: lock(acct) → read → write → unlock
Actor version: send Deposit(50) to account actor

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No lock ordering to get wrong.

check.q: Why doesn't an actor need a lock on its own state?
check.a: Only the actor touches its state, and it processes one message at a time, so there is never concurrent access.

anatomy-of-an-actor.core: An actor has an address, a mailbox and behaviour with private state. On each message it can do three things: send messages to actors it knows, create new actors, and decide how it will handle the next message (change state or behaviour). Everything else, such as location, threads and scheduling, is hidden by the runtime.

first_principles.problem: A developer treats actors like objects and calls their methods directly, breaking isolation.
derivation: Let the runtime **schedule** actors onto threads.

analogy.title: A post-office box with a resident
analogy.story: You know the box number, not where the person lives. They read mail one letter at a time and can reply, hire help or change their habits.
analogy.breaks: People multitask; an actor handles exactly one message at a time.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: State changes only inside receive; `become` swaps behaviour.

check.q: What are the three things an actor can do in response to a message?
check.a: Send messages, create new actors, and designate the behaviour for the next message.

the-let-it-crash-philosophy.core: Rather than wrapping every line in defensive error handling, let-it-crash says: when an actor hits an unexpected state, let it die and have something else restart it in a known-good state. Bugs from corrupted state are wiped out by restarting, and recovery logic lives in one place (the supervisor) instead of being scattered through business code.

first_principles.problem: Error-handling code is longer than the business logic and still misses cases, leaving actors in half-broken states.
truths: Unexpected errors can't all be anticipated.
A fresh start clears corrupted state.

analogy.title: Turning it off and on again
analogy.story: IT doesn't debug every glitch on your laptop; a reboot restores a known state, and most problems vanish.
analogy.breaks: Reboots lose your unsaved work; actors must persist what matters before crashing.

example.title: Parser actor
flow: Supervisor restarts it with empty buffer

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One bad message doesn't poison the system.

check.q: What must be true for let-it-crash to be safe?
check.a: Actors are isolated and any state that must survive is persisted or recoverable, so a restart loses nothing important.

supervisor-hierarchies.core: Actors form a tree: every actor's parent supervises it. When a child fails, the parent chooses a strategy: resume, restart the child, restart all siblings (when they depend on each other), stop it, or escalate the failure to its own parent. Restart limits stop crash loops by escalating once a child fails too often.

first_principles.problem: A database connection actor crash-loops forever, flooding logs without the system ever reacting.
truths: Related actors may need joint restarts.
Repeated failure means a deeper problem.
derivation: Set **max restarts in a time window**.

analogy.title: A management chain
analogy.story: A team lead fixes small problems, restarts a team if members depend on each other, and escalates to their boss when it keeps happening.
analogy.breaks: Managers make judgement calls; supervisor strategies are fixed rules.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: More than 5 restarts in 10 s escalates to the parent.

code.text:
init([]) ->
    SupFlags = #{strategy => one_for_one, intensity => 5, period => 10},
    Children = [#{id => db_conn, start => {db_conn, start_link, []}},
                #{id => cache,   start => {cache,   start_link, []}}],
    {ok, {SupFlags, Children}}.

check.q: When would you use all-for-one instead of one-for-one?
check.a: When sibling actors depend on each other's state, so one failing leaves the others inconsistent and they should restart together.

flavors-of-actors-akka-vs-orleans.core: Classic actors (Erlang/OTP, Akka) are created and supervised explicitly: you manage their lifecycle and location. Virtual actors (Microsoft Orleans, Dapr) always conceptually exist; the runtime activates them on demand by identity, places them on a node, and deactivates idle ones. Classic gives control; virtual gives simplicity at cluster scale.

first_principles.problem: A team spends weeks building sharding and lifecycle code for millions of per-user actors in Akka.
derivation: Use **Akka Cluster Sharding** for similar behaviour.
Choose by need for **control vs convenience**.

analogy.title: Hiring staff vs a temp agency
analogy.story: You hire, manage and fire your own staff; or you call the agency by role name and someone always turns up.
analogy.breaks: Agencies can run out of temps; virtual actors are limited only by cluster capacity.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No spawn or placement code; the runtime handles it.

check.q: What does 'virtual' mean in Orleans virtual actors?
check.a: Actors always logically exist by identity; the runtime activates and places them on demand and deactivates them when idle.
